journal_name: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel categorical framework for reasoning about resources in concurrent programming languages, fundamentally reorienting how we conceptualize linear and affine type systems. Traditional approaches treat resource usage as a discipline imposed upon existing semantics; we instead derive resource awareness as a consequence of monoidal structure in the underlying computational model. Our framework, called Stratified Session Calculus (SSC), replaces the conventional channel-based communication primitives with morphisms in a symmetric monoidal category equipped with additional algebraic structure capturing session types. This formulation enables a clean separation between the behavioral protocol specification (session types) and the physical resource management (linearity), revealing deep connections between classical linear logic and modern session type theory. We establish fundamental results including a canonical cut-elimination procedure that simultaneously manages resource consumption and preserves communication protocols. The metatheory scales to higher-order sessions through an adjunction between the category of session types and the underlying function space. Our work suggests that categorical semantics provides not merely an alternative representation but a genuinely more powerful reasoning tool for next-generation concurrent languages, potentially unifying previously disparate approaches to resource-sensitive programming. We demonstrate the framework's expressiveness by encoding representative examples from the literature, obtaining elegant semantic accounts where previous treatments required ad hoc constructions.

We present a substantial improvement to the precision and scalability of CFL-reachability-based program analysis through a novel decomposition technique that exploits the structural properties of source programs. While context-free language reachability has proven effective for interprocedural dataflow analysis, existing algorithms suffer from either quadratic time complexity or significant precision loss when handling realistic programs with deeply nested calls and complex aliasing patterns. Our approach decomposes the input program into control-flow regions exhibiting specific CFL-closure properties, allowing us to apply specialized algorithms optimized for each region's structure. We introduce the notion of separable paths and prove that any valid interprocedural path can be uniquely decomposed into a composition of separable paths, enabling a divide-and-conquer strategy for CFL-reachability computation. The key insight is that this decomposition preserves the essential structure needed for precision while dramatically reducing the working set size of the reachability engine. We prove that our algorithm runs in O(n³) time in the worst case while achieving precision equivalent to the best existing cubic algorithms, and demonstrate experimentally that the practical performance is substantially better due to the decomposition's cache-friendly access patterns. The technique applies uniformly across a wide range of CFL-reachable analyses including alias analysis, pointer analysis, and taint tracking, making it a practical contribution to the program analysis toolbox.

We present Lumen, a new programming language and runtime system designed from first principles for approximate computing, where applications can trade precision for performance in well-defined, controlled ways. Unlike existing approaches that retrofit approximate computation onto conventional architectures through annotations or library calls, Lumen makes approximate computation a fundamental language construct. The core innovation is a type system based on accuracy types that tracks the propagation of approximation through programs, providing programmers with fine-grained control over which computations may be approximated while guaranteeing that approximation boundaries remain semantically coherent. Lumen's operational semantics define a novel abstraction called accuracy regions, allowing precise specification of which program fragments execute approximately and under what conditions. The runtime system implements a hardware-software co-design with a configurable accuracy controller that manages power-performance-accuracy tradeoffs dynamically based on program-level accuracy specifications. We provide a complete reference implementation including a compiler front-end with accuracy type inference, an optimizer that exploits approximation opportunities identified by the type system, and a runtime that manages heterogeneous execution across approximate hardware units. Our evaluation on a suite of recognition, mining, and synthesis applications demonstrates that Lumen programs achieve an average 3.2× speedup with less than 5% quality degradation compared to fully precise execution, while the type system prevents dangerous accuracy violations that plague ad hoc approximation strategies.

We describe an improved runtime system for virtual machine execution that achieves significant performance gains through adaptive optimization guided by lightweight runtime profiling. While sophisticated just-in-time compilation has achieved remarkable results, existing systems treat compilation decisions as largely static, making them at profile deployment time. Our system, AdaptiveJ, introduces a continuous feedback loop between runtime behavior and optimization decisions, enabling dynamic adjustment of compilation strategy based on actual execution characteristics. The key mechanism is a hierarchical feedback architecture where the runtime collects fine-grained type and call-site information, synthesizes this into higher-level behavioral models, and feeds these models to a cost-sensitive compilation scheduler. We observe that many programs exhibit phase behavior that current systems handle poorly; AdaptiveJ explicitly detects phase transitions and adjusts optimization aggressiveness accordingly, avoiding over-investment in rarely-executed code while re-compiling frequently-executed code more aggressively. The runtime maintains a lightweight representation of the optimization landscape that is updated incrementally as the program executes, enabling rapid response to changing conditions without significant overhead. Our implementation integrates with a production-quality JVM and demonstrates 15-25% performance improvements on standard benchmarks while maintaining predictable pause times suitable for interactive applications. The system scales gracefully with core count, showing improvements even on highly parallel workloads where contention typically limits adaptive optimization effectiveness.
